findings.title: Client mutation breaks on 204 No Content response
findings.rationale: The server returns 204 No Content with an empty body. The client calls `res.json()` unconditionally, which throws a SyntaxError on an empty body. The mutation always rejects, so `onSuccess` never runs and the button never works. This breaks the deployed caller (the FindingsPanel component).

findings.title: Client mutation does not surface errors as ApiError
findings.rationale: The mutation uses raw `fetch` and does not check `res.ok`. On a non-2xx response (e.g., 404, 500), it calls `res.json()` and returns the error body as success data, then invalidates queries. This violates the project's pattern of throwing `ApiError` from `apiFetch` (rule 3 of api-contract-house-rules). The user would see a generic error or stale data instead of the server's error message and code.

matched_title: Client calls `res.json()` on a 204 response, which always throws

findings.title: Client calls `res.json()` on a 204 response, which always throws
findings.rationale: The server returns HTTP 204 No Content with an empty body. The client hook calls `res.json()` unconditionally, which will throw a `SyntaxError` because there is no JSON to parse. This means the mutation always fails on success, breaking the entire feature for every user. The caller that breaks is the web client (FindingsPanel button). Compatible alternative: either have the server return a JSON body (e.g. `{ success: true }`) and parse it, or check `res.ok` and return `null` for 204, or use the existing `apiFetch` helper which handles 204 correctly.

findings.title: Client does not throw `ApiError` on non-2xx responses
findings.rationale: The hook uses raw `fetch` and does not check `res.ok`. On a 4xx or 5xx response, `res.json()` will attempt to parse the error body, but if the body is not JSON (e.g. a plain text error), it throws a generic `SyntaxError`. Even if the body is JSON, the error is a plain `Error`, not `ApiError`. This violates rule 3 (ApiError) of the repository's contract house rules: client code must throw `ApiError` so that pages can display the server's error code and message. The caller that breaks is the web client (FindingsPanel button) – it will show a generic error message instead of the server's details.

matched_title: Client calls `res.json()` on a 204 No Content response, causing runtime error on every success

findings.title: Client calls `res.json()` on a 204 No Content response, causing runtime error on every success
findings.rationale: The server route returns HTTP 204 with no body (`reply.code(204)`). The client mutation function calls `res.json()` on the response, which will throw a SyntaxError because the body is empty. This means every successful call to the endpoint will reject the mutation, the `onSuccess` callback will never run, and the UI will show an error state. The feature is completely broken.

findings.title: Client does not surface errors as `ApiError` on non-2xx responses
findings.rationale: The mutation function uses raw `fetch` and, on a non-2xx response, calls `res.json()` and returns the error body as the mutation result. This means the mutation will resolve with the error object as data, the `onSuccess` callback will run (invalidating queries), and the error will not be surfaced to the user. The repository's pattern (rule 3) requires throwing an `ApiError` on non-2xx responses so that the UI can display the server's error code and message. This is a secondary issue; the primary critical bug above masks it in practice because the 204 case always throws first.

This causes the mutation to fail, `onSuccess` never runs, and the findings panel does not refresh. The user sees an error instead of the expected dismissal.

findings.title: Client uses raw `fetch` without throwing `ApiError` on non-2xx responses
findings.rationale: The client calls `fetch` directly and does not check `res.ok`. On a non-2xx response, `res.json()` will parse the error body but the resulting value is returned as success data, and no `ApiError` is thrown. This violates the repository rule that client requests surface errors as `ApiError`, causing the UI to show a generic error message and lose the status code and error code.

findings.title: Client mutation fails on successful 204 response
findings.rationale: The server returns HTTP 204 with no body, but the client calls `res.json()` on the response. `res.json()` on a 204 response throws a `SyntaxError` because the body is empty. This causes the mutation to fail on every successful call, so `onSuccess` never runs and the query invalidation never happens. The feature is broken as written.

findings.title: Client does not surface errors as ApiError
findings.rationale: The mutation function does not check `res.ok` and does not throw an `ApiError` on non-2xx responses. Per the repository's convention (rule 3), all client requests that use `fetch` directly must throw `ApiError` with the server's error body so that the UI can display the correct status and error code. Without this, a server error will result in a generic error message and lose the error code.

matched_title: Client hook uses raw `fetch` without error handling and calls `res.json()` on a 204 response

findings.title: Client hook uses raw `fetch` without error handling and calls `res.json()` on a 204 response
findings.rationale: The new `useDismissAllSuggestions` mutation function calls `fetch` directly and unconditionally calls `res.json()` on the response. The server returns 204 No Content, so `res.json()` will throw a SyntaxError (empty body). Additionally, non-2xx responses are not handled: the error body (if JSON) would be returned as data, and the mutation would succeed with error data, or `res.json()` would throw. This violates rule 3 (client requests must surface errors as `ApiError`). The fix should use the existing `apiFetch` helper or at minimum check `res.ok` and throw `ApiError` on failure, and avoid calling `.json()` on a 204 response.

findings.title: React key collision when tags contain duplicates
findings.rationale: The rendered tag chips use `key={tag}`. If a finding's `tags` array contains duplicate strings (e.g., `["flaky", "flaky"]`), React will emit a duplicate-key warning and may render incorrectly. The contract does not enforce uniqueness, so duplicates are possible. Using the array index or a composite key (e.g., `${tag}-${index}`) would avoid this.

findings.title: Server contract updated without matching client copy
findings.rationale: The diff adds `merge_conflict: z.boolean().nullish()` to the server-side `PrMeta` schema but makes no corresponding change to `client/src/vendor/shared/contracts/platform.ts`. Per api-contract-house-rules rule 2, the two copies must be updated together to prevent silent drift. The client will not know about the new field until it is manually synced, which could cause issues if the client later tries to use it or if the server starts sending it and the client's type definitions are incomplete.

findings.title: Duplicate tag values cause React key warning
findings.rationale: The `tags` array may contain duplicate strings (the schema does not enforce uniqueness). Using `key={tag}` will produce duplicate React keys, triggering a console warning and potentially causing incorrect re-renders. Use `key={index}` or a composite key like `${tag}-${index}`.

findings.title: Shared contract changed in only one copy
findings.rationale: The diff adds `merge_conflict` to `PrMeta` in the server copy of the shared contract (`server/src/vendor/shared/contracts/platform.ts`) but makes no corresponding change to the client copy (`client/src/vendor/shared/contracts/platform.ts`). Per the repository's house rules, both copies must be updated together to prevent silent drift between what the server sends and what the client expects. The client will still work because the field is optional/nullish, but the two copies will diverge.

matched_title: Shared contract changed in server copy only; client copy not updated

findings.title: Shared contract changed in server copy only; client copy not updated
findings.rationale: Rule 2 of api-contract-house-rules requires that a change to a file under `server/src/vendor/shared/` be mirrored in the corresponding file under `client/src/vendor/shared/` in the same diff. The diff adds `merge_conflict: z.boolean().nullish()` to the server copy but makes no change to `client/src/vendor/shared/contracts/platform.ts`. The two copies will drift: the client’s type for `PrMeta` will lack the new field, and any future client code that reads `merge_conflict` from a response will fail TypeScript checks or silently treat it as unknown. The field is additive and optional, so no deployed caller breaks today, but the inconsistency is a warning.
